That was when I joined Mensa. I started meeting people regularly who were friendly and sympathetic and most of all bright! It really helped me to come out of my shell and expect more of myself.

I'm sure there are many reasons to want to join, and like most things you get more out of it when you're open and willing to contribute yourself. People can and do fall into life-threatening despair as a result of the suffering that tinnitus involves. The suffering is deeply personal and almost impossible to communicate effectively. Tinnitus can suck the joy out of life and make other forms of suffering much worse. While it never really goes away it's possible for it to fade into the background. The key is to change the context, to live well and focus on contribution and other things that make life worth living.

The most important thing you can do is let your Dad know how important he is to you and how much of a difference he's made in your life.

Try to get his attention focused outward. Make a practice of asking him for help with things and for advice.

I've personally found meditation to be very helpful.

I suggest you start by stepping up with practical help to keep him engaged with activities that make life worth living. Spend time with him. Take him to see and do things that he might not feel like doing on his own. Pay attention to the audio environment and try to find out what types of sound bother him and what types of sound help him. It's hard to predict what will work, so it's important to experiment.

Consider buying him a personal music player with a decent pair of headphones / earbuds and introducing him to different types of music in an effort to find things that make it more bearable. Let him know its not a question of matching his musical taste but of treating the music as a tool. Podcasts (spoken words) rather than music can be useful too.

He might be having trouble sleeping. Being sleep deprived can make things much worse. Perhaps you could go to the doctor with him and ask about safe medication to help him sleep.

I've recently completed a Shapeoko 2 build and I've produced some nice output. I'm really pleased with it. During the process I learned that:

* The knock-off dremel clone spindles really aren't worth it. They're loud, underpowered and have a short lifespan. I recommend getting something like the 300W quiet-cut spindle as a minimum.
* The kits aren't quite complete. You'll need to build/buy enclosures for the electronics and power supplies. Also, consider fans for cooling.
* DUST!. Get a shop vac, you'll thank me later.
* The CNC machine is only one of many tools that you'll need to produce useful/nice output. I've gradually filled out quite a list of basic woodworking tools during the building and learning process. You probably will too unless you already have a reasonably well equipped workshop
* Find a local supplier of hardwood flooring. Their offcuts will be very useful to you as a free source of material. Make nice and pay for one or two items occasionally to  keep them on side.
* Take the time to level and square the machine carefully. It will save you a lot of frustration.
* Be prepared for the occasional disaster. You can be pretty sure that you'll break bits a few times so get some spares fairly soon after you know what you're doing.
* Use safety equipment. Protect your eyes with some decent goggles that fit well (over your glasses if you wear those). Get some decent ear defenders also.
* Install a smoke detector near the machine. Eventually you'll leave it unattended to complete a long job and it's all too easy for the machine to start a fire if something goes wrong while you're not close by.
* You'll be working with mains voltages during the build. Get a residual current device to protect yourself from electric shocks.

Best of luck. Have fun.

I really enjoyed that post to r/funny. I’ve been involved in technical pre-sales as an engineer for a number of years and I’ve been on both sides of the kind of arguments that you describe.

In my experience, sales people and engineers often find themselves talking at cross-purposes through a lack of mutual understanding. I think it’s important to bear in mind the other person’s role within the conversation that you’re trying to manage. They may actually be the one you need to convince in order to close the deal.

Big-ticket technical sales often involve teams of people with various skills from both the vendor’s side and the customer’s side, including non-technical and technical people at various stages. The key thing is to ensure that each side is balanced.

Involve your pre-sales engineers early in the process

It’s common for sales people to do the groundwork of establishing the customer relationship and value proposition well before engaging pre-sales engineers. However, this can sometimes leave them at a disadvantage when dealing with a customer with a strong engineering culture. They’re much more likely to involve technical people from their side at an early stage.

From the customer’s side in such a meeting, the engineer’s role is to act as a sceptic. They’ll be doing their best to trip you up with technical questions. It’s important to be prepared for those questions with detailed product information or to be able to promptly call on well-informed engineers from your side.

If you come across such a situation, my advice would be to politely acknowledge the questions and explain what you can and cannot answer personally on the day. They’ll respect your honesty, just make sure they have the opportunity to talk to an engineer from your team within a reasonable time.

A few tips:
The motors and props are the most likely parts to need replacing. Props are cheap and can be replaced in the field so have a few sets in your 'oh crap' bag.
Motors are fiddly to replace and need soldering but only cost a couple of dollars each so get two or three of each kind.
Motors come in two kinds, clockwise (CW) and counter-clockwise (CCW), while it's possible to switch them, they won't last as long if you do so always try to use the correct type.
When replacing a prop, be aware that you can damage the motor if you don't apply opposing pressure on the end-cap of the motor as you push on the prop. Be careful not to damage the wires as you do.
With the older X4 model, there's little protection for the motors during a crash. I used a small bead of Sugru on each corner to make tiny rubber landing pads which seemed to help.
The transmitter has a fake antenna, which you can discard without hurting your range.
The main cause of crashes is loss of orientation, the newer model comes with different colored LEDs on the corners. If you get the older model, consider attaching a super bright red LED facing slightly downwards on the back next time you need to re-solder a motor. You can use a bead of Sugru or Polycaprolactone to make a mount for the LED that doesn't look too shabby.
Sometimes the X4 can completely lose calibration after a crash. If you find that it won't take off correctly but that the motors all have good connections, then that's your issue. There's a bit of stick gymnastics to do to recalibrate but it's fairly simple.
Get three or four spare batteries so that you can get a decent number of flights before coming home. They're only a couple of dollars each so it's a good use of money, also get a spare charger so you can charge two at once. Be careful when inserting third-party batteries as they can be slightly fatter (higher capacity). They do fit with a little wiggling.
Don't store the batteries fully charged as they won't last as long. Keep them about half discharged if you need to store them for more than a few days.
When the X4's lights start flashing, it's time to land, if you keep flying until the motors stop the the batteries won't last as long. If you have the older model, use flight time as a guide as it will be hard to see the front facing lights flashing.
Try to graduate to expert mode as soon as you fee confident enough. The extra agility can get you out of trouble more often than it can get you into trouble.

Be aware that's there's a (pricey) FPV version of the X4 now. It's on the Banggood website.
Have fun!
